extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and constitutional framers (People of the State of New York) considering the structure and powers of the federal judiciary
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and constitutional criteria for structuring the national judiciary: tenure, compensation, scope of jurisdiction, organization of courts, and accountability mechanisms. Written as arguments to inform ratification and institutional design decisions for the U.S. federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency of judicial office / life tenure
rubrics_metrics.description: That inflexible and uniform adherence to the rights of the Constitution, and of individuals, which we perceive to be indispensable in the courts of justice, can certainly not be expected from judges who hold their offices by a temporary commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodical appointments (temporary commissions) undermine judicial independence by creating incentives to please the appointing authority (executive, legislature, or popular sentiment). Permanency in office promotes impartial adherence to the Constitution and laws, deters corrupt or partisan behavior, and attracts men of requisite integrity and long legal training who would otherwise avoid giving up lucrative practice for short-term posts. The Convention therefore properly adopted tenure during good behavior (life tenure) as essential to judicial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed provision for judges' support / non-diminishable compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The judges of the United States 'shall at stated times receive for their services a compensation which shall not be diminished during their continuance in office.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A provision guaranteeing compensation that cannot be diminished protects judicial independence by preventing the legislature from coercing or punishing judges via pay cuts. While exact fixed amounts are inadmissible in the Constitution due to changing values, the arrangement permits legislative adjustment upward as circumstances require but forbids reducing the allowance of any sitting judge. This differs from the President (whose salary neither can be increased nor diminished during the term) because judges hold office for life and may require raises over long tenure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment for malconduct as the constitutional accountability mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges "are liable to be impeached for malconduct by the House of Representatives, and tried by the Senate; and, if convicted, may be dismissed from office, and disqualified for holding any other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impeachment is presented as the only constitutionally consistent means of holding judges responsible without undermining independence. It supplies the essential precaution for accountability while preserving tenure and non-diminishable compensation; other removal schemes would threaten impartiality and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of general removal-for-inability provisions and age limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of a provision for removing the judges on account of inability has been a subject of complaint... The mensuration of the faculties of the mind has, I believe, no place in the catalogue of known arts... An attempt to fix the boundary between the regions of ability and inability, would much oftener give scope to personal and party attachments and enmities than advance the interests of justice or the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing judges for 'inability' (other than obvious insanity) would be arbitrary and susceptible to partisan abuse; objective measurement of mental faculties is impractical. Age-based removals (e.g., an upper age limit of sixty) are criticized as inhumane and unnecessary because many judges retain deliberative faculties well beyond such limits and may depend on the office for livelihood. Thus, general removal-for-inability rules and mandatory retirement ages are discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of federal judicial authority — enumerated classes of cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal judiciary ought to extend to: (1) cases arising out of the laws of the United States; (2) those which concern the execution of the provisions expressly contained in the articles of Union; (3) those in which the United States are a party; (4) those which involve the peace of the Confederacy (relations with foreign nations or among States); (5) those which originate on the high seas and are of admiralty or maritime jurisdiction; and (6) those in which the State tribunals cannot be supposed to be impartial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are justified as necessary to give effect to national laws and constitutional restrictions, preserve uniformity in interpretation, maintain public peace between states and with foreign nations, and provide impartial forums where state courts would be biased. The enumerated list is presented as constituting the entire mass of judicial authority appropriate for the Union, subject to legislative exceptions and regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial power must be able to enforce constitutional restrictions uniformly
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought always to be a constitutional method of giving efficacy to constitutional provisions... The mere necessity of uniformity in the interpretation of the national laws decides the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where states are prohibited from certain acts by the Constitution, federal courts must have authority to enforce those prohibitions. Uniform construction and application by federal tribunals prevent contradictory decisions by multiple independent courts that would undermine the Constitution's efficacy (the 'hydra' of inconsistent final jurisdictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of equity jurisdiction alongside legal jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: It has also been asked, what need of the word 'equity'. What equitable causes can grow out of the Constitution and laws of the United States?... In such cases, where foreigners were concerned on either side, it would be impossible for the federal judicatories to do justice without an equitable as well as a legal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts should exercise both law and equity powers because many disputes (fraud, trusts, unconscionable bargains, land conveyances under competing state grants) require equitable remedies. Equity jurisdiction is particularly important in cases involving foreigners or matters that legal remedies alone cannot satisfactorily resolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal adjudication for disputes affecting interstate or international peace and privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: The peace of the WHOLE ought not to be left at the disposal of a PART... the national judiciary ought to have cognizance of all causes in which the citizens of other countries are concerned... To secure the full effect of [privileges and immunities], it is necessary that its construction should be committed to that tribunal which, having no local attachments, will be likely to be impartial between the different States and their citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matters implicating foreign relations, treaties, and disputes between states or their citizens require national tribunals to preserve the Union's peace and public faith. Federal courts are better positioned to interpret privileges and immunities impartially and to prevent state-level evasion of national obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: One Supreme Court of final jurisdiction distinct from the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: "The judicial power of the United States is to be vested in one Supreme Court, and in such inferior courts as the Congress may, from time to time, ordain and establish." The ultimate decision in causes should rest in a distinct judicial body rather than within a branch of the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A separate Supreme Court prevents the intermixture of legislative and judicial functions that could lead to biased interpretation of laws by those who made them. Judges, selected for legal knowledge and granted tenure, are better suited to final adjudication than legislators lacking legal expertise and subject to partisan marshaling. The arrangement also mirrors several state constitutions and is defended as preferable to vesting final judicial power in a legislative body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial interpretation guided by the Constitution as the supreme standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution ought to be the standard of construction for the laws, and wherever there is an evident opposition, the laws ought to give place to the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts must interpret statutes consistently with constitutional principles. This authority is not a novel or dangerous prerogative unique to the proposed federal plan but follows from the theory of a limited Constitution and applies equally to state judiciaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional checks (impeachment, comparative weakness) limit judicial usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular misconstructions and contraventions of the will of the legislature may now and then happen; but they can never be so extensive as to amount to an inconvenience... The inference is greatly fortified by the consideration of the important constitutional check which the power of instituting impeachments... would give to that body upon the members of the judicial department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fears of judicial encroachment are overstated because courts lack force to sustain usurpations and are checked politically by impeachment powers. These structural features provide sufficient remedy for occasional judicial errors without subjecting judges to legislative control that would compromise independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to constitute inferior federal courts to decentralize federal jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of constituting inferior courts is evidently calculated to obviate the necessity of having recourse to the Supreme Court in every case of federal cognizance. It is intended to enable the national government to institute ... a tribunal competent to the determination of matters of national jurisdiction within its limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing inferior federal courts reduces burden on the Supreme Court and creates appropriate forums in each State or district for federal causes. Congress should be able to ordain such courts as needed to administer national jurisdiction effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying solely on State courts for national causes due to local bias and varying competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the fitness and competency of those courts should be allowed in the utmost latitude, yet ... the substance of the power in question may still be regarded as a necessary part of the plan, if it were only to empower the national legislature to commit to them the cognizance of causes arising out of the national Constitution... There are ... substantial reasons against such a provision: the most discerning cannot foresee how far the prevalency of a local spirit may be found to disqualify the local tribunals for the jurisdiction of national causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State courts may be unsuitable channels for national matters because of local attachments, prejudices, or structural differences among state judicial systems; therefore the federal legislature should retain explicit authority to create federal courts rather than depend entirely on state tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges require extensive legal learning and reliance on precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: A voluminous code of laws is one of the inconveniences necessarily connected with the advantages of a free government... it is indispensable that they should be bound down by strict rules and precedents... the records of those precedents must unavoidably swell to a very considerable bulk, and must demand long and laborious study to acquire a competent knowledge of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because adjudication under a complex body of laws depends on mastery of voluminous precedents and technical rules, judges must possess long legal training and experience. This scarcity of highly qualified individuals further justifies permanence of tenure and institutional arrangements that attract and retain such persons.
